parts: This biographical text tells the life of Ustad Bismillah Khan, the shehnai maestro who played for more than eight decades and spread peace and love through music. It shows that hard work is the key to success and that music has no caste or boundaries.

He received the Bharat Ratna in 2001, having earlier received the Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan and Padma Vibhushan — all four top civilian awards. He was born on 21 March 1916 in Dumraon, Bihar, the second son of Paigambar Khan and Mitthan. His ancestors were court musicians of the princely state of Bhojpur, and his father was a musician in the court of Maharaja Keshav Prasad Singh of Dumraon. He was named Qamaruddin (to rhyme with his elder brother Shamsuddin), but his grandfather Rasool Baksh Khan exclaimed 'Bismillah' on seeing him as a baby, and the name stuck.

At six he moved to Varanasi, where his maternal uncle Ali Baksh 'Vilayatu' was the official shehnai player at the Vishwanath Temple. Noticing his keenness, Ali Baksh took him under his tutelage. Bismillah followed his uncle all day to the temples and practised for hours — without play time, school or sometimes even meals. He attained perfection quickly; the flowing waters of the Ganga inspired him to improvise and invent ragas earlier thought beyond the range of the shehnai. He often played at the Vishwanath Temple and was a devotee of Saraswati, goddess of wisdom and arts.

He was almost single-handedly responsible for making the shehnai famous and bringing it into mainstream Indian classical music. His concert at the All India Music Conference in Calcutta (1937) brought the shehnai into the limelight. Despite fame he remained simple: he never collected wealth, lived humbly in Varanasi, and his favourite transport was the cycle rickshaw. He loved his city and motherland so much that he declined an offer of permanent citizenship of the USA. He believed music would survive even if the world perished, believed in Hindu-Muslim unity and often said, 'Music has no caste.'

He played at the Red Fort on the eve of Independence in 1947 and thereafter every 15 August after the Prime Minister's speech. He performed in Afghanistan, the USA, Canada, Bangladesh, Europe, Iran, Iraq, West Africa, Japan and Hong Kong. After his wife died he called his shehnai 'begum'. He died of a cardiac arrest on 21 August 2006 at the age of ninety; the Government declared a day of national mourning, and he was buried with his shehnai under a neem tree in Varanasi with a 21-gun salute from the Indian Army.
Dedication and hard practice; simplicity; love for the country; communal harmony through music.
